strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: improving multi-task robotic manipulation under partial observability. Selecting task-conditioned virtual views from an aggregated RGB-D point cloud is intuitive and potentially useful.

The framework combines view selection, coarse-to-fine action prediction, and task-conditioned sparse experts in a coherent pipeline. The three-stage training procedure and loss/reward components provide a plausible implementation direction.

The main evaluation covers 18 diverse RLBench tasks. TAVP obtains an average success rate of 86.7%, compared with 84.9% for ARP+, with particularly notable gains on Insert Peg (96.0% versus 78.4%) and Sort Shape (64.0% versus 46.4%).

The paper reports useful supporting measurements, including sensitivity to view count and radial range, an inference-time comparison (0.436 s versus 0.394 s for ARP+), and limitations involving point-cloud quality and reflective or transparent objects.
The manuscript is generally organized around a clear motivation, overview diagram, formal camera parameterization, and readable main results table.
weaknesses: The central framing as active view planning is materially overstated. TAVP does not acquire new observations from movable cameras: it aggregates four fixed RGB-D views and re-renders that existing point cloud from virtual poses. Reprojection cannot recover surfaces absent from the original measurements, so claims that the method actively acquires information or overcomes fixed-camera occlusion are not technically supported as written.

The evidence does not isolate the benefit of learned view planning. The only corresponding ablation replaces learned views with random viewpoints, causing success to collapse from 86.67% to 8.89%. A controlled comparison using the same TAVP architecture, capacity, training procedure, and canonical fixed views is missing. Consequently, the 1.8-point gain over ARP+ cannot confidently be attributed to MVEP rather than architecture, capacity, or training differences.

The principal improvement is modest and lacks uncertainty estimates. Evaluation appears to use only 25 episodes per task, with no independent training seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. This is especially consequential when the average gain over ARP+ is 1.8 percentage points and TaskMoE contributes only 0.88 points in Table 2.

Several conclusions contradict the reported numbers. TAVP does not outperform ARP+ on every task: it is worse on Open Drawer, Place Cups, Screw Bulb, Stack Cups, and Sweep to Dustpan, among others. Likewise, the claim that increasing the number of views consistently improves all five validation tasks is false: from K=3 to K=4, Put Groceries in Cupboard falls from 16% to 4% and Close Jar from 76% to 52%.

The zero-shot evidence is too weak for the broad generalization claim. It evaluates one nominally unseen task over 25 episodes and obtains only 12% success. The manuscript does not explain how a new task identifier is handled by a router explicitly conditioned on task ID, nor whether the task or closely related variations appeared elsewhere in training.

TaskMoE is insufficiently specified and analyzed. The manuscript does not clearly define the experts, router computation, assignment of tasks to the eight gates, placement of all TaskMoE modules, parameter counts, load-balancing behavior, or how routing operates for unseen task IDs. There is also no matched-capacity dense control or analysis of learned expert specialization.

The PPO formulation is incomplete and internally unclear. The pseudo-environment algorithm provides no next observation, termination signal, trajectory construction, or advantage computation; it calls the storage an experience replay buffer despite PPO being on-policy. The paper also labels reward weights learnable without specifying their optimization objective, and invokes reparameterized sampling even though its role in PPO is unexplained.

The real-world evaluation is qualitative only. Although five tasks and 100 training demonstrations per task are described, the paper gives no number of test trials, success rates, variance, or aggregate baseline comparison. Selected success sequences cannot substantiate real-world robustness.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate: the claimed code link is only the placeholder text “TAVP”; important supervised-training settings are deferred to another method; PPO hyperparameters and reward weights are absent; and the manuscript alternates between 86.44% and 86.67% for the full model.

The bibliography contains obvious template or placeholder references, including “Frobnication” entries and a Face and Gesture submission placeholder. This is a serious manuscript-quality issue rather than a minor stylistic refinement.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: improving visual representations for multi-task manipulation under occlusion. Combining task-conditioned expert routing with learned virtual viewpoints is a potentially useful direction.

The method is evaluated per task on 18 RLBench tasks rather than only reporting an aggregate score. TA VP improves the reported mean success rate from 84.9% for ARP+ to 86.7%, with notable gains on insert peg, put in cupboard, and sort shape.

The manuscript includes component ablations, viewpoint-count and camera-radius sensitivity experiments, and an inference-time comparison. It also acknowledges dependence on accurate point clouds and difficulty with reflective or transparent objects.
The three-stage training procedure and the broad pipeline are presented clearly at a high level, and the qualitative figures help communicate the intended behavior.
weaknesses: The central active-view claim is not convincingly supported. TA VP does not acquire new observations: it reconstructs a point cloud from four fixed RGB-D cameras and renders virtual views of those same observed points. Reprojection cannot recover geometry occluded from every input camera, so statements that the method overcomes fixed-camera occlusion and actively acquires information are materially overstated. This limitation is especially important because the motivating problem is missing observations.

The experiments do not isolate the contribution of learned view planning. The key ablation replaces learned views with random views, which collapses performance to 8.89%, but there is no comparison to the fixed canonical views used in Stage 1 while holding the complete TA VP architecture and training protocol constant. Random, potentially poor camera poses are not an adequate control. Consequently, the gain attributable to MVEP rather than TaskMoE, architecture, capacity, or fine-tuning remains unknown.

Several empirical claims contradict Table 1. TA VP does not outperform ARP+ on every task: it is worse on open drawer, place cups, screw bulb, stack cups, and sweep to dustpan, and ties on additional tasks. The claimed improvement of “up to +56%” is also not obtained against the stated strongest baseline ARP+; the largest absolute gains over ARP+ are 17.6 points. These are substantive mischaracterizations rather than presentation issues.

The reported overall gain is small relative to the uncertainty of the evaluation: 86.7% versus 84.9%, with TA VP apparently evaluated on only 25 episodes per task. No confidence intervals, repeated training seeds, significance tests, or variance are reported. Per-task TA VP results occur in four-point increments, making many highlighted four-point gains only one additional success. It is also unclear whether all baselines were retrained under identical data, evaluation episodes, and inputs.

The real-robot evidence is inadequate for the robustness and practical-generalization claims. Although five tasks and 100 training demonstrations per task are described, the paper reports no number of evaluation trials, quantitative success rates, uncertainty, or systematic baseline comparison. A single TA VP/ARP+ qualitative example cannot establish real-world improvement.

The claimed zero-shot generalization is weak and under-specified. Performance on one unseen task, open drawer, is 12%, corresponding to only 3 successes in 25 episodes, with no uncertainty or comparison to a competitive transfer baseline. More fundamentally, routing explicitly uses a task ID and a task-to-gate structure, but the manuscript does not explain how an unseen task ID is assigned to one of the learned gates. Calling this a “performance breakthrough” and evidence of meaningful generalization is unsupported.

Core technical details are missing or inconsistent. TaskMoE lacks precise expert architectures, insertion locations, routing equations, task-to-gate assignment or learning procedure, balancing losses, parameter counts, and handling of unseen tasks. The loss-difference reward r0 is defined as a four-component vector but subsequently treated as a scalar reward; the learnable reward weights are not given a learning objective. The paper also invokes reparameterization for end-to-end backpropagation while stating that MVEP is optimized with PPO, without reconciling the two.

The reward and view geometry are insufficiently justified. Negative heatmap entropy can reward confidently wrong predictions; cosine distance between camera-pose parameter vectors is not clearly a meaningful geometric view-diversity measure; and the look-at construction can become singular when the up vector is parallel to the viewing direction, with no stated safeguard. No ablation separates the task-loss, entropy, and diversity reward terms.

The MoE benefit is marginal in the main experiment: removing TaskMoE lowers mean success only from 86.67% to 85.56%. There is no parameter- or compute-matched dense control, routing visualization, expert-utilization analysis, or direct evidence that task interference is reduced. Thus the claimed representation disentanglement is not demonstrated.

Reproducibility is poor. The manuscript provides a placeholder code link, refers to videos that are not part of the presented evidence, and omits important supervised-training details by deferring to prior work. It also retains dummy template references [1–6], contains inconsistent averages such as 86.44% versus 86.67%, and uses imprecise language such as evaluating on “25 demonstrations” rather than episodes. These issues further reduce confidence in the reported study.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: fixed projections can make manipulation policies sensitive to occlusion, and task-aware virtual viewpoints are a plausible way to expose useful geometry from a fused RGB-D point cloud.

The overall system is conceptually coherent, combining coarse grounding, viewpoint selection, task-conditioned sparse experts, fine grounding, and action prediction. The three-stage training procedure is also reasonably motivated.
Evaluation covers 18 diverse RLBench tasks. TAVP improves average success from 84.9% for ARP+ to 86.7%, with particularly large gains on insert peg, sort shape, and put in cupboard.

The paper reports useful sensitivity and efficiency measurements. Increasing inference time from 0.394 s to 0.436 s is modest, and the analysis of viewpoint count and radial constraints exposes meaningful operating tradeoffs.
The manuscript includes clear system diagrams, per-task results, limitations, and a small real-robot demonstration that qualitatively illustrates the intended benefit.
weaknesses: The evidence does not adequately support the broad performance claims. The average gain over ARP+ is only 1.8 percentage points, yet no multiple-seed results, confidence intervals, significance tests, or matched-trial analysis are reported. With only 25 evaluation episodes per task, a single outcome changes a task score by four points.

The claim that TAVP achieves higher success across all tasks is factually inconsistent with Table 1. It is substantially worse than ARP+ on stack cups (60.0% versus 80.0%) and is also worse on open drawer, place cups, screw bulb, sweep to dustpan, and other tasks. These regressions deserve analysis.

The central active-exploration ablation is not diagnostic. Replacing learned views with random views and observing 8.89% success shows that arbitrary projections are harmful, but it does not isolate the benefit of MVEP relative to the strong fixed-view rendering used by ARP+ or the Stage-1 TAVP model. A fixed-view, matched-capacity ablation is necessary to substantiate the claimed contribution.

The method selects virtual renderings from a point cloud reconstructed using four fixed RGB-D cameras; it does not acquire new physical observations. Consequently, it cannot recover surfaces absent from the original point cloud. The paper repeatedly describes this as active camera exploration or acquisition without clearly separating viewpoint reprojection from physical sensing.

TaskMoE is insufficiently specified and weakly isolated. The paper does not clearly explain how tasks are assigned to the eight gates, how unseen tasks obtain a task identifier or gate, what each expert contains, or whether load-balancing and capacity constraints are used. Its main ablation gives only a 1.11-point gain, while the separate five-task experiment reports a much larger change under a different setup without explaining the discrepancy.

The zero-shot claim rests on only 3 successes out of 25 trials on one task. The protocol is ambiguous because open drawer is also part of the main 18-task training suite, and the mechanism for routing its unseen task ID is unspecified. This is not sufficient evidence for generalization.

The PPO formulation lacks important technical details. The vector-valued loss difference in Eq. 6 is not reduced to a scalar reward, the learnable reward weights are not constrained or described, and PPO optimization details such as clipping, value loss, entropy coefficient, rollout/update schedule, and number of samples are omitted. Calling the fixed-view reference loss a lower bound is also unjustified.

Real-world evidence is qualitative only: no number of test trials, success rates, baseline aggregates, variability, or failure analysis is provided. Individual successful sequences cannot establish robustness or sim-to-real effectiveness.

Reproducibility is presently limited. Stage-1 and Stage-3 hyperparameters, architecture and parameter counts, gate construction, rendering implementation, training duration, and baseline retraining protocol are missing. The displayed code link is merely labeled “TAVP,” and the bibliography still contains six placeholder template references.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: fixed viewpoints can provide incomplete evidence for manipulation, and jointly adapting visual representations and virtual viewpoints is a useful research direction.
The proposed combination of a learned multi-view exploration policy with task-conditioned sparse experts is coherent and moderately original relative to the RVT-2/ARP foundations.

Evaluation includes 18 RLBench tasks, module ablations, viewpoint sensitivity analysis, latency measurements, data-size analysis, and five real-world tasks. The reported RLBench average of 86.6% exceeds ARP+ at 84.9%, while latency rises only from 0.394 s to 0.436 s.
The fixed-view ablation reaches 83.33% versus 86.67% for the full method, providing some direct evidence that learned viewpoint selection contributes beyond the remaining architecture.
weaknesses: The principal framing is misleading: MVEP does not actively acquire new sensor observations. It re-renders an already aggregated point cloud constructed from fixed RGB-D cameras, so it cannot recover surfaces occluded from every input camera. This materially weakens claims that the method overcomes occlusion through dynamic camera exploration, particularly in the real-world setup where no physical camera-motion protocol is described.

The central PPO formulation is insufficiently specified and contains ambiguities affecting technical correctness. Equation 6 subtracts two vectors of four losses without defining their scalar reduction; Equation 8 describes cosine distance between camera positions but uses p, previously defined as a five-dimensional pose parameter including radius and up-vector angles; the learnable reward weights, PPO value model, probability treatment after sigmoid-bounding, and training settings are not given. Consequently, the method cannot be reliably reconstructed.

TaskMoE is also underspecified: the manuscript does not explain how tasks are assigned to the eight gates, whether assignments are learned, how routing is performed for an unseen task ID, where experts are inserted, or whether load-balancing/capacity losses are used. The claimed discovery of latent task clusters is not directly evaluated. Its main 18-task ablation gain is only 1.11 points, from 85.56% to 86.67%.

The empirical claims overstate the evidence. TAVP does not outperform ARP+ on every task as stated; it is worse on several tasks, including Meat off Grill, Put in Safe, Screw Bulb, Stack Blocks, and Sweep to Dustpan. The overall gain is only 1.7 points, with no matched-seed statistical analysis and no clear account of whether all baseline results use identical data and evaluation protocols.

The real-world evidence is too weak to establish the strong robustness claims: each result uses only 10 trials, uncertainty is omitted, and the only tabulated baseline is Diffusion Policy despite TAVP using a different ARP-derived policy stack. Moreover, Figure 5 and its discussion identify the real-world baseline as ARP+, contradicting Table 4. Performance remains only 20% under heavy occlusion and 30% under illumination changes.

The zero-shot conclusion rests on one task and a 12% success rate over 25 trials versus 0%, without uncertainty or comparison to chance and alternative transfer baselines. Calling this a generalization breakthrough is unsupported. Similarly, the data-efficiency differences largely overlap the reported standard deviations.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the point-cloud encoder/aggregation into the stated MLP, detailed network architectures, expert and gate training, loss aggregation, optimizer settings for stages 1 and 3, PPO hyperparameters, reward weights, evaluation seeds, and parameter counts are missing. The displayed project/code reference is only the placeholder 'TAVP'. Dummy template references [1–6] and multiple terminology/figure inconsistencies are presentation problems, but the missing implementation details are a material issue.

strengths: The combination of learned virtual-view selection and task-conditioned sparse experts addresses a relevant problem: fixed projections and cross-task interference in multi-task manipulation.
The simulation evaluation covers 18 RLBench tasks, and the reported 86.6% average exceeds ARP+ by about 1.7 percentage points. Particularly large gains appear on Insert Peg and Sort Shape.
The paper includes several useful diagnostics: fixed/random-view ablations, viewpoint-count and radius sensitivity, latency, data efficiency, and small real-robot robustness tests.
The fixed-view ablation is informative: success decreases from 86.67% to 83.33%, suggesting that learned view selection provides some benefit beyond the underlying action model.
The main pipeline and motivation are generally understandable, and the appendix supplies camera parameterization and selected training hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The central framing is materially misleading. TAVP does not actively acquire new observations or move a physical camera: it first aggregates RGB-D data from four fixed cameras in simulation or three fixed cameras in the real world, then renders virtual projections of that same point cloud. Re-rendering cannot recover geometry absent from the original fixed views, so claims about overcoming occlusion by active sensing or increasing scene coverage are not established.

The average RLBench improvement over ARP+ is modest (86.6% versus 84.9%) and lacks a statistically adequate comparison. The paper does not state the number of seeds behind TAVP's deviations, while ARP+ entries have no uncertainty. TAVP is also worse than ARP+ on multiple tasks, including Open Drawer, Place Wine, Put in Safe, Screw Bulb, Stack Cups, and Sweep to Dustpan, contradicting the claim that it is better across all tasks.

The ablations do not cleanly substantiate both proposed components. Removing TaskMoE changes the 18-task average by only 1.11 points, with no uncertainty or capacity-matched dense control. The dramatic random-view failure is a weak control; the relevant fixed-view comparison shows only a 3.34-point gain. There is no comparison against simple heuristic view selection, view ensembling, or learned attention over the original camera observations.

The purported zero-shot result is not convincing: 12% on only 25 Open Drawer trials corresponds to three successes, no confidence interval is reported, and the procedure for routing an unseen task through a module that explicitly consumes a task ID is unspecified. Calling this a generalization 'breakthrough' is unsupported.

The PPO formulation is technically underspecified and internally unclear. The pseudo-environment is a one-step offline supervised-loss evaluation rather than an interactive environment; the necessity of PPO versus direct differentiable optimization is not justified. Equation 6 subtracts vectors of heterogeneous losses but subsequently treats the result as a scalar reward, and the learning and normalization of reward weights, value function, rollout construction, and PPO objective are omitted.

TaskMoE is insufficiently specified for verification or reproduction: the expert architecture, gate assignment or learning mechanism, load-balancing objective, expert insertion locations, token-level versus sample-level routing, parameter counts, and compute-matched baselines are absent. The claimed discovery of latent task clusters is not analyzed.

The real-world evidence is too small and poorly controlled for the strong robustness claims. Each percentage is based on only 10 trials, without uncertainty, and the sole baseline is Diffusion Policy rather than the ARP+-based architecture used to isolate the proposed additions. Camera inputs, training parity, model capacity, and evaluation randomization are not documented adequately.

There is an internal experimental inconsistency: the real-world discussion and Table 4 compare against Diffusion Policy, whereas Figure 5 labels the real-world baseline as ARP+. This makes the qualitative comparison difficult to interpret.

Reproducibility is weak. The manuscript contains only a placeholder project link ('TAVP'), provides incomplete optimization details, and does not adequately document real-world protocols or baseline retraining. It also retains irrelevant template references [1]-[6], indicating insufficient manuscript quality control.

Overall, the idea and preliminary results are worthwhile, but the mismatch between active-sensing claims and virtual re-rendering, coupled with underspecified methodology and insufficiently controlled evidence, currently outweighs the contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical limitation of robotic manipulation systems: fixed observations can obscure task-relevant objects and the end effector. Combining task-conditioned viewpoint selection with specialized multi-task representations is well motivated and relevant to computer vision and robotics.

The proposed framework is technically coherent. MVEP predicts multiple constrained camera poses from an aggregated RGB-D point cloud, while TaskMoE conditions sparse expert routing on task identity, language, and visual context. The three-stage training scheme provides a plausible way to learn view selection from offline demonstrations.

The evaluation is reasonably broad: 18 diverse RLBench tasks, five real-robot tasks, robustness tests, data-efficiency analysis, latency measurements, and sensitivity experiments. This is substantially stronger evidence than simulation results on only a few selected tasks.

TAVP obtains the best reported average RLBench success rate in Table 1, improving from 84.9% for ARP+ to 86.6%, with particularly large gains on Insert Peg and several occlusion-sensitive tasks. The fixed-view ablation reaches 83.33% versus 86.67% for the full system, directly supporting the value of learned viewpoints.

The real-world study is encouraging: TAVP achieves 88% average success versus 68% for Diffusion Policy across five tasks, and remains stronger under changes in instances, backgrounds, objects, occlusion, and illumination. Although small, this study demonstrates that the approach is not restricted to idealized simulation.

The measured inference overhead is modest: latency increases from 0.394 s for ARP+ to 0.436 s for TAVP. The qualitative examples also clearly illustrate how alternative rendered views can recover useful spatial context.
weaknesses: Several conclusions are overstated. TAVP does not outperform ARP+ on every task, contrary to the text: it is worse on tasks including Place Cups, Place Wine, Put in Safe, Screw Bulb, Stack Blocks, and Stack Cups. The average improvement is only 1.7 percentage points, and uncertainty or matched-run significance is not reported for the ARP+ comparison.

The main comparison does not fully isolate the two contributions. TaskMoE adds only 1.11 average points in the 18-task ablation, without error bars, while the fixed-view versus active-view difference is 3.34 points. Ablations separating TaskMoE in perception from TaskMoE in the action policy, controlling parameter count, and comparing against simpler learned or heuristic view-selection methods are absent.

The claimed zero-shot generalization is supported by only one task and 25 episodes: TaskMoE succeeds in 3 of 25 trials versus 0 of 25 without it. This is suggestive but insufficient to establish broad unseen-task generalization, particularly without confidence intervals or comparisons to dense parameter-matched alternatives.

Important methodological details are underspecified. The paper does not precisely define the TaskMoE router, task-to-gate assignment, expert architectures, balancing regularization, or how a previously unseen task identifier is routed. Likewise, the PPO objective, value-function optimization, update schedule, and procedure for learning the reward-component weights are omitted.

There are mathematical ambiguities in MVEP training. Equation 6 subtracts vectors of heterogeneous losses but subsequently treats the result as a scalar reward. Equation 8 refers to camera positions while writing cosine distance between p_i vectors, which were defined as five-dimensional spherical pose parameters; cosine similarity in that parameterization is not geometrically meaningful unless a conversion is performed. Degenerate look-at/up-vector configurations are also not discussed.

The method performs virtual re-rendering from a point cloud reconstructed using four fixed RGB-D cameras, rather than physically acquiring new observations. It can improve presentation of already observed geometry but cannot reveal surfaces occluded from every input camera. Some language about active camera exploration and overcoming occlusion should therefore be qualified.

The real-world evidence uses only 10 trials per task and a single Diffusion Policy baseline, leaving substantial statistical uncertainty and making it difficult to separate viewpoint planning from backbone or capacity differences. The robustness experiment is similarly small, and absolute performance under heavy occlusion and illumination variation remains low at 20% and 30%.

Reproducibility is weakened by the placeholder project link, incomplete training specifications, absence of parameter counts and training cost, and erroneous placeholder references [1–6]. These are partly presentation issues, but the missing architectural and optimization details materially impede faithful reproduction.
